text.text:
These appear to be a series of yellowed documents, loosely tagged together, dated from May through September 1936. The first is a hastily scrawled letter from a Massachusetts father to his son, imploring the latter to pause his studies at the University of Madrid and promising to finance his passage back to the United States, or to take up his residency at one of a truly excessive number of French or British universities.
The subsequent reply is neatly laid alongside, in which the man’s son promises that he has dutifully heeded his father’s wishes, assures him that he is more than able to cover the cost of tuition at Bordeaux, and that he is eagerly looking forward to returning stateside.
A cheery postcard is stapled to the letter, bearing a depiction of the… Eiffel Tower? This is followed by a thick wedge of similar cards marching through January-September, bearing such choice messages as, 'I have learned the true joy of French baguettes,' 'Wish mom was around to see the Arc de Triomphe,' and 'University has stolen my time, the local señoritas have stolen my heart.'
The final document in the pile is a letter on official U.S. government letterhead, from the U.S. embassy in Madrid.
'It is the regrettable duty of this consular office to inform you that your son, <full_name> of <random_number><random_number><random_number>, <city>, Massachusetts, has been killed in the active fighting in Madrid after not heeding this embassy’s instructions to leave Spain. He was last reported seen tending to wounded militia fighters on the grounds of Ciudad Universitaria, moments before nationalist mortar fire levelled the tent and adjoining areas.'

This appears to be a well-aged letter from July 1936, penned by a New England preacher to his nephew. Certain choice passages read:
'It is my hope that God, in His boundless wisdom and benevolence, shall keep His watchful eye upon you, and that you, in turn, shall keep Him in your heart for the challenges ahead.'
'Do not heed the vulgar propaganda of those Bolshevik scum who condemn violence with their lips, yet allow their rabble to burn, torture, and murder the children and homes of God. Madrid shall fall, and righteousness shall prevail.'
'Do not lose hope, dear nephew, and do not associate yourself with the Republic, Bolsheviks, Jews, and, indeed, your university friends should they decide to take up arms on behalf of sin. When Franco shall take Madrid, allow yourself into the trust of his soldiers, for they are gentlemen.'
The document clearly shows signs of having been crumpled.

This is a neatly penned letter dated early August 1936, originating from a Catholic pastor in Vermont.
<given_name>,
I hope you have never known me to be hyperbolic, nor given to panic, so take me seriously when I write that I fear Spain. I fear that, once again, war is not far from Europe’s shores. Above all, I fear for yourself, and for the innocent. France, Belgium, or Spain—the country may change, but war does not.
There is much talk here. The radioman claims that terrible atrocities have been wrought upon churches and followers of the Lord by those loyal to the Republic. How much of it is true, I do not know. Rumour has a way of growing teeth. Still, it has found a ready ear among the folk down at Lenard’s, and the reverend has even set up a collection tin to fund guns for Franco. God forgive us—I doubt it will come to much, but the very notion...
Either way, evil is not solved by outcompeting it with further evil. Enclosed, I am sending my old .45. It, and prayer, saw me through more than a few hurdles at Belleau Wood, and I hope it serves you just as well. You well know Córdoba will be next in line on Franco’s march. Come what may, I expect you to do your duty to the Lord and your fellow man, and to protect those around you should the time come. Our faith is judged in Heaven alone, and not at the point of a would‑be dictator’s gun.
War does not change. I can only pray that the hearts of good men do not either.'

This is a hefty folio of letters exchanged between two women from the summer through winter of 1936. Skimming the correspondence, it appears that both had children traveling through Spain at the outbreak of the war.
'It is my deeply held conviction that they cannot possibly be dead. I can feel it in my bones and within my soul. So many months have passed—surely we would have heard something by now. <given_name> is clever, as is my <given_name>, and I am convinced that they are far too sensible to have gotten caught up in anything. Likely, they are simply in Portugal or France, having a laugh at our expense as we fret ourselves to death over them. Have faith; surely we will hear from them.'
There is only one further letter, dated a week later from the same woman. In it, she jubilantly exults that her child has written to her after arriving in New York. Anxiously, she enquires if her correspondent had received any news of her own.
No reply was ever sent.

This is a stack of letters exchanged between a husband and wife across late 1936. Reading them, you piece together that the wife, clearly bedridden and suffering from some terminal illness, was corresponding with her husband, a businessman in France. Apparently, the couple had lost touch with their daughter, who had been living in Spain at the outbreak of the insurgency.
Page after page shows the wife’s ever more feeble and incoherent pleas to find their daughter, interspersed with reassuring telegrams and letters from her husband. Nearing the end of the stack, you find a letter signed by the couple’s daughter, assuring her mother of her safety and well-being. The reply is written in such a weak hand that only fragments are legible: 'knew you’d,' 'thank you,' 'love,' 'at peace.'
An obituary note for the woman is attached to the sheet via tags, showing that she passed peacefully the very next day.
Even to your eye, it is obvious that the daughter’s and husband’s handwriting are exactly the same.
